1 big thing: America's not ready for space war
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

The future of war is in outer space — and the U.S. is unprepared for the fallout.

Why it matters: An outbreak of space warfare would cripple the global economy by disrupting satellites used for everything from worldwide financial transactions to maritime navigation. It would also hinder the U.S. military's ability to conduct some of its key missions on Earth.

  • The dependence on satellites is precisely what makes them tempting targets for foes.
  • China has made major advancements, such as satellites with robotic arms that could disable U.S. equipment and lasers that can blind military space sensors.
  • Russia lags behind, but U.S. officials fear it may unleash an orbital nuclear weapon that "could pose a threat to all satellites and to the space-enabled services the world depends on."

What they're saying: Todd Harrison, the American Enterprise Institute's space expert, told me "we've been under the illusion" that an adversary would target only military satellites and leave civil or commercial ones alone. That's no longer the case.

  • "In a future conflict, we could very well see the civilian and commercial space infrastructure that we often take for granted ... being attacked," Harrison said. "Is the American public ready for that? I'm not sure they are."
  • "We're quickly coming to the conclusion that there's no sanctuary in space, not even in a small conflict," he added.

Threat level: Last month, U.S. officials revealed that the military had weapons in space — a bombshell admission they said was aimed at deterring adversaries.

Yes, but: Doug Loverro, a former top NASA and Pentagon space policy official, said the deterrence effect is "partially the case, but not really true."

  • China and Russia have long assumed the U.S. has had space weapons, he said. In future wars, if adversaries feel they can't gain the upper hand against the U.S. military, infrastructure like GPS could be targeted, Loverro added.

State of play: Aerospace analysts warn the nation isn't prepared if China or Russia destroys U.S. satellites. They say the defense industry lacks the critical supplies and personnel to fight back.

  • The space industry is "running hot at peak demand, yet structurally fragile beneath the surface," warned PwC and the Aerospace Industries Association in the intro to a March report — in other words, U.S. space needs are outpacing equipment supplies.
  • The U.S. also likely lacks skilled engineers needed to rebuild its space assets after a crisis, RAND researchers said.

Zoom in: The U.S. has more than 13,000 operational satellites, up from just 670 a decade ago, per AEI's Space Data Navigator. China has more than 1,400 sats — almost as many as all non-U.S. NATO countries combined.

  • Yes, but: Those numbers can be misleading. China and Russia are working to close the gap in certain fields by expanding launch cadence, growing orbital constellations and developing anti-satellite prototypes.

The bottom line: The military is preparing for space wars, but the nation isn't ready for their consequences.

  • Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation's chief director of space security and stability, told me the U.S. may be "ready to start a war" but added, "I don't know that we're ready to finish a war in space."
 
 
2. Watch this "space"
 

A Falcon 9 rocket launches from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Jan. 4. Photo: Gwendolyn Kurzen/DVIDS
 

Unmanned military spaceplanes launching mysterious objects into orbit. Satellites targeting satellites. Spacecraft hunting each other down like fighter jets.

  • This isn't science fiction. They're real-world examples of how China, Russia and the U.S. are trying to gain a strategic edge in space.

Why it matters: As the world's superpowers compete for orbital superiority, military, government and industry leaders are readying for space warfare.

📩 Every Thursday, we'll unpack the strategy, geopolitics and innovation propelling warfare into space.

Topics we'll cover include:

  • Rocket dreams: National security demand for launch has skyrocketed, and it isn't slowing.
  • Emerging tech: Companies are developing everything from maneuverable spacecraft to orbital cargo vehicles to meet military needs.
  • Hypertransparent warfare: Commercial satellite imagery has changed the battlefield by providing unprecedented levels of intelligence.
  • Orbital debris: Spent rockets, decommissioned satellites and other human-made obstacles are cluttering orbit, making access to space more difficult.
  • Space law: Cold War-era treaties partly police space conflicts, and as orbital warfare evolves, international law will have to catch up.

🚀 The bottom line: These topics, like space, are always expanding. Is there something we're missing? Let us know!
 
 
3. Exclusive: SPACECOM's "gaps"
 

Gen. Stephen Whiting. Photo: Derek Lacey/Axios
 

The four-star general leading the military's high-stakes space missions sees critical gaps in the nation's arsenal to counter China's and Russia's emerging threats.

Why it matters: Gen. Stephen Whiting, head of U.S. Space Command, has seen orbital threats evolve rapidly during his 37-year military career. In an exclusive chat with me, he said the command needs more investment and capabilities.

  • The ongoing war in Iran has revealed that U.S. adversaries are targeting ground-based radar systems to gain an advantage. Whiting said the same logic now applies to the nation's military assets orbiting Earth.

What he's saying: "Some of those key gaps are self-protection of our high-value assets on orbit," Whiting said.

Zoom in: Whiting has emphasized that the military needs to be able to counter a foe's fleet of low-Earth orbit satellite constellations. It also requires enhanced orbital detection to identify threats.

  • A larger arsenal of equipment to destroy satellites with physical or electronic damage is also crucial, he added.
  • "I will always ask for more because I believe that promotes deterrence," Whiting said. "But also, if we are to have a conflict in space — and that is not inevitable — it gives me a greater range of options to fulfill our American objectives."

What's next: Whiting is stepping down as the head of SPACECOM in the coming months and wrapping up his nearly four-decade-long military career. As he looks back on his time in uniform, he said he has "great optimism" about the U.S. position in space.

  • "I think we're well postured. We certainly have challenges," Whiting said, "but this is the team I would want to be on for that future."

4. Rocket Lab's reach
 

Electron launches from Rocket Lab Complex 2 on Wallops Island, Virginia. Photo: Courtesy of Rocket Lab
 

President Trump put the space rocket industry on notice in August when he set an audacious annual goal of 1,000 U.S. rocket launches and reentries by 2030 — a roughly 460% increase from last year.

Why it matters: To meet Trump's mandate, America needs more launch sites — especially for top national security missions.

What they're saying: The rocket industry should mirror the commercial airline business — meaning launch regulations need to change, Rocket Lab's vice president of global launch services, Brian Rogers, tells Axios.

  • Rogers said Rocket Lab gave feedback to the FAA and the Commerce Department about sticking points that hinder launch expansion.

The big picture: U.S. National Security Space Launch missions are currently limited to Florida's Cape Canaveral and California's Vandenberg Space Force Base.

  • Rocket Lab is expanding its footprint in Virginia and Alaska. This summer, the company unveiled GHOST: a containerized launch site that allows rockets to send payloads into orbit from anywhere.

Zoom in: Rocket Lab launches its suborbital HASTE and small-lift Electron rockets from its complex at the Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport on Wallops Island, Virginia.

  • The company said yesterday its medium-lift Neutron rocket is targeting an inaugural launch out of Wallops next year. When Neutron eventually launches for its first NSSL mission, it will be the first time in the program's history that a mission launches outside of Florida and California, the company said.
  • Later this year, Rocket Lab will start its first mission for a program of suborbital launches for Space Systems Command's Rocket Systems Launch Program. Most of those will take place from the Pacific Spaceport Complex-Alaska. That same infrastructure can also be used for larger orbital missions in the future.

The bottom line: Space superiority isn't possible without launch.
 
 
5. Quick hits
 

Space Force Tech Sgt. Kyle Yeager adjusts the tilt of a helical antenna in preparation for a training exercise with the AC-130J Ghostrider at Cannon Air Force Base, New Mexico. Photo: Natalie Vandergriff/DVIDS
 

🪖 The U.S. Army had a successful demo with Amazon's low Earth orbit satellite network at Maryland's Aberdeen Proving Ground.

  • What's next: Amazon and the Army are planning "more advanced tests," the company announced during the AUSA conference this week.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: SpaceX dominates this market. The Army demo gives Amazon steam as it plans to unveil its internet service later this year.

📡 Ukraine's sudden Starlink restrictions are undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia, my colleague Barak Ravid reports.

  • Driving the news: Service partially returned yesterday, but Ukrainian officials want answers.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: The incident shows that Starlink has become a crucial national security asset, and interference can cause havoc.

🆕 Space Force now has its own special operations headquarters, according to an internal memo.

  • The big picture: The new component field command will weave the Space Force into more missions.
  • 💭 My thought bubble: Last year, lawmakers questioned the component's standup. It appears that's changed.
 
 
6. Full circle
 

Thomas Novelly during a 2024 Pentagon press briefing. Screenshot: Defense Department
 

🔭 One of the first Space Force stories I wrote revealed that some Americans struggled to believe the service branch was real.

Now, most of my decade reporting has been spent covering the Space Force's evolution from Colorado to Capitol Hill.

  • 📰 I started writing about the military in 2019 at South Carolina's Post and Courier newspaper.
  • ☢️ It was there that I first ran into Colin, who was crushing nuclear national security coverage at the Aiken Standard.

If you would've told me then that I'd be his co-worker and covering space warfare ... now, that I wouldn't have believed.
